message:
QUESTION:
Which supplier, A or B, should the firm use for component K-220, given that a delivery taking longer than 26 days causes a stockout?

DATA:
Choosing a supplier for component K-220. Safety stock covers lead times of up to 26 days. Any delivery that takes longer than 26 days causes a stockout, which halts the assembly line.

Last 12 orders from each supplier, lead time in days (order placed to goods received), in date order:
Supplier A (sea freight): 21, 23, 22, 24, 20, 22, 45, 23, 21, 22, 24, 21
Supplier B (road and rail): 18, 19, 30, 17, 29, 18, 31, 19, 28, 18, 30, 19

Notes:
- A's 45-day delivery was the order shipped in February, during the documented three-week national port strike, which delayed all sea freight that month. There has been no strike since, and none is planned.
- B had no comparable disruption. B's deliveries of 28 days or more are spread throughout the year.
- Unit price: A £4.10, B £4.05. Annual volume about 40,000 units.
- Both suppliers meet the quality specification for K-220.
- This decision applies to K-220 only. Other components are bought under separate contracts with different specifications, volumes and routes.

KNOWN FLAWS:
F1. [calculation] B's 12 lead times sum to 276, so the mean is 23.0 days, not 22.0. CORRECTION: B mean 23.0 days, one day quicker than A's 24.0 (A sums to 288).
F2. [omission] Ignores that the 45-day delivery was caused by a documented one-off national port strike that delayed all sea freight. CORRECTION: Excluding the strike order, A's other 11 deliveries average 243/11 = 22.1 days (below B's 23.0), with a maximum of 24 days and no deliveries over 26.
F3. [method] The stockout criterion depends on how often lead time exceeds 26 days, not on the mean or the single worst case. CORRECTION: Exceedances over 26 days: A 1 of 12 (8%, the strike order), B 5 of 12 (42%: 30, 29, 31, 28, 30). B caused a stockout on 5 of its last 12 orders. Choose A.
F4. [inference] Generalises from one component's lead-time record to other components with different specifications, routes and contracts. It also rests on the flawed conclusion that B is better. CORRECTION: The data say nothing about B's performance on other components. No recommendation beyond K-220 is supported.

EXTENSIONS:
- Quantify the cost trade-off: B saves £2,000 a year on price, against stockouts on about 5 in every 12 orders, each of which halts the line. Even a modest cost per stockout outweighs the saving.
- Note that B's lead times look bimodal (17-19 days or 28-31 days). Ask B what drives the slow orders (e.g. consolidation or rail scheduling); if the cause is controllable, B could become viable, perhaps with a longer order cycle.
- Model safety stock directly: to cover B's observed maximum of 31 days, cover would need to rise by 5 days (about 550 units at 40,000 a year), with holding cost that can be set against the price difference.

FINAL VERSION:
**Recommendation: Supplier A.** In normal conditions A delivers within the 26-day cover. B exceeds it on about two orders in five, and possibly one in two. B's 5p price advantage is too small to pay for those stoppages.

## Lead-time reliability

**Supplier A.** Eleven of A's 12 deliveries took 20–24 days, leaving at least 2 days of margin inside the cover. The one exception took 45 days. That order shipped in February, during the documented three-week national port strike that delayed all sea freight that month. There has been no strike since and none is planned. The strike was an external event and does not show how A normally performs.

**Supplier B.** B's lead times fall into two groups, with nothing between 19 and 28 days:
- a fast group at 17–19 days
- a slow group at 28–31 days

Every slow order exceeded the 26-day cover. That was 5 of 12 orders, or about two in five.

From order 3 onward, every other order was slow (orders 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11). Orders 1 and 2 were both fast. This pattern suggests a recurring cause, such as alternating routes, carriers or depots, rather than random delay. Twelve orders cannot prove this, but nothing in the data suggests it will stop. If the pattern continues, B's future breach rate would be nearer **one in two** than two in five.

## Why the simpler measures point the wrong way

| | Mean (days) | Worst case (days) | Range (days) | Deliveries over 26 days |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A, all 12 orders | 24.0 | 45 | 20–45 | 1 (strike) |
| A, excluding strike order | 22.1 | 24 | 20–24 | 0 of 11 |
| B | 23.0 | 31 | 17–31 | 5 of 12 |

Across all 12 orders, B looks better on mean, worst case and range. None of these measures reflects what actually stops the line:
- **Mean.** B's fast deliveries cancel out its slow ones in the average, but the line stops on every slow delivery.
- **Worst case and range.** A looks worse only because of the single strike-affected order. Without it, A's worst case is 24 days.

The measure that matters is the number of deliveries over 26 days. On that measure A is clearly better.

## Is the difference just chance?

Twelve orders per supplier is a small sample. Even so, A had 0 breaches in 11 normal orders, against 5 in 12 for B. If both suppliers really had the same breach rate, a split this uneven would be unlikely (Fisher's exact test, one-sided, p ≈ 0.02).

This result depends on excluding the strike order. If that order counts as a breach (1 in 12 against 5 in 12), p ≈ 0.08, which is not significant at the 5% level. Excluding it is justified: the strike was a documented one-off event that affected all sea freight. The gap between the suppliers is large either way, but formal significance relies on treating the strike as exceptional.

## Price

B is 5p per unit cheaper (£4.05 against £4.10, about 1.2%). At about 40,000 units a year, that saves about £2,000 annually.

B comes out ahead only if that £2,000 exceeds the cost of B's extra stoppages. Using B's record of about 5 stoppages per 12 orders:

| Orders per year | Expected B stoppages per year | B wins only if each stoppage costs less than |
|---|---|---|
| 12 (monthly) | about 5 | about £400 |
| 52 (weekly)* | about 22 | about £90 |

Order frequency is not given, so these figures are illustrative. If B's breach rate approaches one in two, both thresholds fall further. Stopping an assembly line almost certainly costs more than either figure.

\*The weekly row applies the brief's rule that every delivery over 26 days causes a stockout. With weekly ordering, several orders would be in transit at once, and a later order arriving early might sometimes cover a late one. That would reduce B's actual stoppages and raise the weekly threshold. The monthly row has no such overlap, so £400 per stoppage is the safer benchmark.

## Quality

Both suppliers meet the K-220 specification, so quality does not separate them.

## Risks and caveats

- **Strike exposure.** A relies on sea freight and remains exposed to port disruption. No strike has occurred since February and none is planned, but a future one cannot be ruled out.
  - *Main mitigation:* when port disruption is signalled, temporarily raise safety stock to cover the expected delay.
  - *Secondary option:* move orders to B. On its own this does not solve the problem, because B's breach rate is about 40–50% unless safety stock is also raised.
- **Small sample.** Twelve orders per supplier is limited evidence, and formal significance depends on how the strike order is treated. Quarterly monitoring will show whether the difference holds.
- **B could improve.** B could become competitive if it finds and fixes the cause of its 28–31-day deliveries. Alternatively, B would become workable if safety stock covered about 32 days, but the extra inventory has its own cost. Both options are worth revisiting at the next review.

## Scope

This decision covers K-220 only. Other components are bought under separate contracts with different specifications, volumes and routes. This data says nothing about which supplier suits those components, so it should not be used to consolidate them with either supplier.

## Actions

1. Award the K-220 contract to **Supplier A**.
2. Review lead-time performance quarterly. Track the **number of deliveries over 26 days**, not the average.
3. Keep **Supplier B** as a qualified back-up. Pair any switch to B with a temporary increase in safety stock.
4. Ask B why every other delivery from order 3 onward has been slow, and whether this reflects alternating routes, carriers or depots. Reconsider B if it fixes the cause.
